1:
The opening formula is disputed before the sentence is. Robertson (grammatical-historical) holds that faithful is the saying points backwards here, unlike its use earlier in the letter, and should close the previous paragraph; Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports that several of the Greek fathers joined it to the last verse of the preceding chapter and referred it to the doctrine there; Gill (reformed) records the same opinion and then decides for the other side, that it looks forward. Calvin (reformed) names Chrysostom as holding the backward reading and rejects it outright: Paul commonly uses the phrase as a prelude to what he is introducing, and the preceding discourse needed no such strong affirmation, whereas what follows is weightier. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes it forward too and adds a suggestion about its origin: the saying was probably current among the brethren and may have belonged to their liturgy, perhaps to a prayer that volunteers might present themselves for what was then a dangerous office.

Why the subject arises here at all is answered the same way by two witnesses. Calvin gives three reasons: that it might be seen why women were refused so arduous a work, that nobody should conclude their exclusion admitted all men indiscriminately, and that Timothy should be reminded what watchfulness the election of bishops requires. His summary is that so far are women from being fit for the office that not even men are to be admitted to it without distinction. Gill puts the same transition briefly — the work belongs to men, but not to every man — and takes the formula as a call for attention to something beyond controversy.

On the word desire the witnesses are struck by the same oddity. Clarke observes that both Greek verbs denote eager, even passionate wanting, and finds it strange that the episcopate should have been coveted when it meant labour, want, persecution and death without income; from which he concludes that these words were designed more for later ages than for that one. Robertson supplies the grammar — a condition assumed as true, and a verb of reaching out after a thing used only twice more in the New Testament — and notes that the noun for the office is late and rare outside the Greek Bible, meaning over-seership. Chrysostom (eastern-antiochene) makes the distinction that governs everything after: he does not blame the desire, because the office is a work of protection, and the man he acquits is the one who wants to protect the Church rather than to covet dominion and authority. Even Moses, he says, desired the office without the power, and got for it the taunt at Acts 7:27, who made thee a ruler and a judge over us.

That the office is a good work is where they converge, and each presses it his own way. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) calls it an excellent but laborious work. Clarke says a work it then was, heavy, incessant and painful, and that there were no unpreaching prelates in those days and should be none now. Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes the contrast between the centuries explicit: the office may now be thought a good preferment, but then it was thought a good work, and ministers should look more to the work than to its honour. Calvin hears in the Greek adjective an allusion to the old proverb that excellent things are difficult, so that the word joins the difficulty to the excellence. Barnes (grammatical-historical) reads the verse as a general commendation set before the list of qualifications, establishing that what is sought is itself desirable. Henry adds the claim that the following verses assume: the office is of divine appointment and not of human invention, it existed before any magistrate countenanced Christianity, and the minister should never be the tool of the state.
2:
Blameless is the first requirement and the witnesses agree on its limit. Gill (reformed) says it cannot mean free from sin or blameless before God, but blameless before men and not chargeable with any notorious crime, and hears an allusion to the priests of the law who had to be without blemish. Barnes (grammatical-historical) notes that the Greek word differs from the one translated blameless elsewhere, and does not demand perfection: it demands a man against whom no charge of immorality or false teaching can be laid. Robertson (grammatical-historical) renders it not to be taken hold of. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) presses the metaphor to a skilled boxer who so guards himself that his antagonist cannot land a blow. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) adds why it matters: not only believers but those outside must respect such a man, since a society of this kind was certain to provoke distrust.

What bishop means is settled before it is disputed. Clarke traces the word back through the Septuagint to a Hebrew term for a visitor who personally inspects those he presides over, and observes that Paul applies it to the elders of Ephesus at Acts 20:28. Robertson is blunter: it does not carry in the New Testament the monarchical sense it has in Ignatius, of a bishop set over elders. Ellicott writes throughout of the presbyters or bishops as one class.

Then the phrase that has divided the church. Ellicott reports the ancient consensus: the oldest writers, the decisions of councils, and the continuing custom of the Greek Church all read it as barring a second marriage in a candidate, remarriage disqualifying for the higher grade. Robertson answers in three words, one at a time. Chrysostom (eastern-antiochene) had already taken it that way: the apostle is not requiring a bishop to have a wife but forbidding him more than one, since the Jews were allowed both second marriages and two wives at once — though he notes that some read it as requiring the one wife. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) is the most emphatic against Ellicott’s reading: it neither means that a bishop must be married nor that he may not marry a second time, which is as lawful as a first and may in some cases be a duty; what it excludes is the polygamy and easy divorce common among Jews and heathens alike, from which ministers above all must stand clear. Barnes declines to require marriage — however desirable he thinks it in general — and reports the dispute rather than closing it.

The vices follow, and here the witnesses part again. Barnes takes the word behind not given to wine as describing one who sits by it habitually, and grants that it does not by itself prohibit wine; but he reads Paul’s manner as disapproval and holds that no minister is obliged to touch it while many have ruined themselves by it. Gill will not go so far: what is forbidden is immoderate and continual drinking, and wine is lawful for such men and sometimes necessary. Ellicott shifts the ground entirely, holding that drunkenness is scarcely in view and the warning is against choosing a man who frequents noisy banquets where imprudent words are spoken. Clarke reports a scholar’s case that the word means imperious and insolent whether through wine or otherwise, and Gill records versions that render it the same way. On the next term Clarke is at his sharpest, taking no striker to forbid not only blows but the persecution of those who differ, with an example of a bishop who beat the men he examined when argument failed him; Ellicott extends it to wounding a soul with cutting words. Both then note that the clause about filthy lucre is absent from the older manuscripts, Clarke listing the versions that omit it even while expounding it.
4:
Gill (reformed) settles what house means: the family, wife, children and servants, not the man’s own body kept under. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) describes the rule wanted — not sternness or tyranny but government by rule, each member knowing his place — and holds that no family prospers that is not under subjection. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) fixes the purpose: the standard must be no inimitable one but an example any honest man may copy, so the test is a well-ordered household rather than an extraordinary life. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes the clause about gravity as a warning that levity undermines domestic authority, and extends it by parity of reason to every parent. Barnes (grammatical-historical) draws a stronger inference than the others will: the verse implies a minister ought to be a married man, since the New Testament supposes one who can be an example in all the relations of life. He then pulls back, allowing that it cannot be insisted on beforehand and binds only a man who has a family — which leaves this and his position two verses earlier in some tension.

The reason given draws the chapter’s best writing. Barnes calls it a beautiful and striking argument and works the analogy both ways: a church resembles a family, though larger and more various, and the minister’s authority is less absolute than a father’s. What they share is a government meant to be paternal, so a man severe, partial or tyrannical at home cannot be expected to preside over the larger household of faith. Ellicott reaches the same point through Theodoret, quoting him to the effect that a man who cannot rule a small community decorously is no candidate for a broader sphere. Clarke makes it a matter of method rather than temper: a disorderly family shows a man with no plan of presiding, and whoever fails there should be trusted with no government, ecclesiastical or civil. Robertson (grammatical-historical) treats the verse as a parenthesis in the list, and notes that no New Testament writer but Paul, at Acts 20:28, describes the church as God’s in this way.

The next disqualification is a metaphor to everyone. Barnes takes novice at its root, a plant newly set and not yet strong enough for storms; the word marks a man young in faith rather than in years, though he allows the reasons to bear against youth too. Gill says the same, one lately come to the truth and newly a member. Ellicott points to the case in front of Timothy: the Ephesian church had stood some years and could supply men of standing, and Timothy himself was young in years but old in trials. Clarke uses the requirement to concede that presbyter and bishop seem to be two names for one office, while adding at once that not all presbyters were bishops, since not all had the qualifications listed here. Robertson gives the word’s vernacular history and glosses the danger that follows as raising a smoke, a screen of pride.

On the condemnation the witnesses agree. Ellicott takes the puffing up as being clouded by an authority no training had fitted the man for, and the judgment as the one God passed on the devil, whose own fall came of the same blinding pride. Wesley says it in a line, that he falls into the same condemnation the devil fell into, and traces the swelling to the new honour and its applause. Robertson makes the grammar explicit, reading the phrase as the condemnation passed upon the devil rather than one uttered by him, and flags that the next verse uses the same construction the other way about. Gill closes on the last requirement: outsiders may dislike a minister’s principles and despise his office, and still cannot help speaking well of a becoming life, which is what brings them to hear him.
8:
Before the qualifications, an absence. Chrysostom (eastern-antiochene) asks why Paul goes straight from bishops to deacons with nothing on presbyters, and answers that the two differed little: both were teachers and presidents in the church, what is said of the one applies to the other, and the bishop’s only advantage is the power of ordination. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) asks the same as a question: where are the presbyters, and could the apostle have passed the order over in silence if it were essentially distinct? On what the deacons did, Henry (puritan-evangelical) and Gill (reformed) agree: the temporal concerns of the church, serving tables while the ministers gave themselves to the word, as at Acts 6. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) traces the order from that appointment and notes that its functions widened as the church grew, until these men assisted the presbyters and often took their place.

On the vices they enlarge rather than divide. Henry derives a double tongue from a double heart and puts flatterers and slanderers under it; Barnes (grammatical-historical) gives its root, saying a thing twice, and its sense, meaning one thing and saying another; Robertson (grammatical-historical) describes a man between two people telling each something different. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says it might be rendered liars. On gain Wesley is the fiercest voice in the chapter: everything got above food and raiment by ministering in holy things is filthier than what is honestly earned emptying sewers.

The mystery of the faith draws two images and a variant. Ellicott calls the mystery a treasure kept in the casket of a pure conscience, and Robertson uses the same figure; both mean that orthodoxy without the life is worth nothing, which Barnes states flatly — a man may be firm in doctrine and corrupt at heart, and should not hold the office even though he does not preach. Gill notes that the phrase itself was used by the ancient Jews. Clarke reports a single manuscript reading the mystery of the resurrection instead, found nowhere else and worth little except as evidence of what one copyist thought Paul meant, and takes the clause about conscience to be aimed at antinomianism. On the trial that follows, nobody claims to know its form: Barnes denies a formal examination and reads it as time enough for a character to become known, Ellicott suggests a probation doing the work before being set apart for it, Clarke wants a spell as a consistent private member, and Robertson records that Paul does not say.

Two questions divide them sharply. The first is whose women are meant. Gill records the deaconess reading and prefers the deacons’ wives; Wesley assumes wives too, faithful to God, their husbands and the poor. Ellicott thinks a solitary charge about wives in the middle of rules for deacons almost decisive against it, and asks why deacons’ wives should be specified when presbyters’ are not; he renders it women in like manner, and reports that Chrysostom and most ancient expositors made them deaconesses. Robertson agrees, comparing Romans 16:1, and suggests that as almoners such women faced special temptations. Clarke takes a third line, that Christian women in general are meant, while allowing that deaconesses would suit the words exactly. Barnes reports the deaconess reading, names Chrysostom among its supporters, and keeps the common one. The second question is what a good degree is. Clarke and Wesley read promotion, a step toward ministering the bread of life rather than bread that perishes, and Clarke takes the boldness as liberty of speech in teaching. Barnes will not go there, the word meaning a step and serving as well for dignity or influence as for office; and Robertson, noting that the inscriptions use it of a foothold though later writers made it a grade, doubts that Paul meant a rank at all.
14:
Paul writes because he may not arrive, and Barnes (grammatical-historical) turns that into an argument. The verse proves, he says, that Paul did not regard Timothy as the permanent diocesan bishop of Ephesus: no bishop would write so to another, nor announce that he expected shortly to come and finish the arrangements himself. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads the clause without polemic and marks the grammar as concessive, and thinks the pressing dangers made Paul doubt the visit would happen at all. Robertson (grammatical-historical) draws another inference from the word shortly: a forger would hardly have written it, since the hope failed and the writer did not know it would. Gill (reformed) and Ellicott agree that these things means the qualifications just given, not the letter at large. Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the purpose plainly: those employed in God’s house must see to their behaviour and not their preaching only, since the office binds a man to good conduct.

What house of God means is settled four times over, with one result. Barnes denies that it refers to a place of worship or to deportment in one, and takes it of the church as a body of believers, God’s residence having moved from the temple to his people. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) works the same allusion from the tabernacle, making every believer a habitation of God through the Spirit. Ellicott traces the Old Testament usage through the Temple to the covenant-people and lands on the congregation. Robertson is the most concrete: the word ordinarily means household, so the sense is the family of God rather than a building, and Christians then had no separate houses of worship, being themselves the sanctuary of 1 Corinthians 3:16. On who is to behave, Ellicott and Robertson part: Ellicott extends it past Timothy to his colleagues and renders it how men ought to behave, while Robertson supplies thee as the more natural subject.

Then the sentence that has divided readers most. Clarke says that never was there a greater variety of opinions on any portion of Scripture than on these two verses, and proposes a reconstruction: take the pillar and ground of the truth with what follows rather than what precedes, so that the mystery, which is the pillar and ground of the truth, is confessedly a great thing. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads it the same way, the mystery being the foundation and support of all the truth taught in the church, and Robertson likewise treats the mystery as explaining the pillar. Ellicott holds the older division, in which the Church upholds the truth pillar-like, the grandeur of the pillar proportioned to what it carries.

On the mystery itself the witnesses divide twice more. Barnes insists that mystery here does not mean unintelligible: what was hidden is now disclosed, and the passage should not be used to prove that anything in the doctrine surpasses comprehension. Gill says the opposite: though revealed and to be believed, the union of the two natures cannot be accounted for by reason. The second division is textual and graver. Ellicott reports that the most ancient authorities read not God but he who was manifested in the flesh, that the later manuscripts and most of the fathers who cite the verse do read God, and that the substitution looks like a well-meant scribal correction rather than doctrinal prejudice. Robertson agrees, rejecting both the received reading and a neuter variant, and follows the critical editors in printing the clause as a hymn fragment in six strophes. Clarke, Wesley and Gill expound the received text as it stands: Gill as the incarnation and the union of two natures, Wesley through all six articles from the form of a servant to the taking up into glory, and Clarke setting the six out as the substance of the mystery he has redefined.
